title: SRE SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives, and Runbooks
author: Ari Chen
body:
Overview

Purpose: This document defines Redwood Inference's standard approach to SRE documentation covering SLO definition and measurement, error budget policy and response, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling, and runbook structure. It codifies concrete thresholds, ownership, and procedures so teams can reliably operate and evolve production services.

Scope
- Applies to: user-facing inference APIs (text-generation, chat, embeddings), control plane services (routing, quota, billing), and infra components (GPU pools, KV cache).
- Excludes: local developer tooling and non-critical internal analytics pipelines (those have separate SLOs documented under eng-platform).

1) SLO Principles and Measurement
- Guiding principles:
  - Measure user-visible reliability and latency where customer impact is direct (API success & latency).
  - Keep SLOs simple to reason about and actionable (single metric + window).
  - Provide separate SLOs for availability, latency, and correctness where appropriate.

- Standard SLOs (default for new services unless otherwise approved):
  - Availability (production-hosted API endpoints): 99.95% monthly uptime for non-batch endpoints (error defined as 5xx or 4xx that indicates service failure).
  - Latency (generation endpoints): p95 < 250ms for lightweight models (<= 8k tokens); p95 < 700ms for heavy/long-seq models.
  - Embeddings endpoint: p95 < 150ms; availability 99.99% monthly.
  - Control plane critical paths (auth, routing): 99.9% monthly availability.
  - Background/async batches: throughput SLA and job success rate 99% daily.

- Measurement details:
  - Windowing: SLOs are computed over a 30-day rolling window by default; quarterly SLO rollups used for reporting to leadership.
  - Error budget unit: 1 minute of unavailability measured by configured checks or a failed request ratio depending on metric.
  - Data sources: primary: Prometheus metrics (request_total, request_errors, request_duration_seconds), secondary: distributed tracing and synthetic canaries (Grafana Cloud synthetic checks).
  - SLO query examples (PromQL):
    - Availability: (sum(rate(request_total{job=\"api\"}[30d])) - sum(rate(request_errors{job=\"api\",code=~\"5..\"}[30d]))) / sum(rate(request_total{job=\"api\"}[30d]))
    - Latency p95: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{job=\"api\"}[5m])) by (le))

2) Error Budget Policy and Response
- Error budget calculation:
  - Budget = (1 - SLO) * window_length. For a 99.95% SLO over 30 days, monthly error budget ~21.6 minutes.

- Burn stages and actions (standardized):
  - Normal (<= 25% burn): normal ops, monitor. On-call follows standard alerting.
  - Elevated (25% - 50% burn): notify product & platform; hold non-critical deploys; investigate trends and capacity.
  - High (50% - 75% burn): immediate mitigation plan, halt feature rollouts, require follow-up postmortem within 3 business days.
  - Critical (>75% burn): paging for incident response lead, rollback any risky changes in last 24h, engage platform SRE and product leadership; freeze releases until error budget restored.

- Who acts:
  - Service owner (primary): owns mitigation and communications.
  - On-call SRE: execute runbooks, scale or failover per playbooks.
  - Platform SRE: assist with fleet-level capacity, fallbacks, and cross-service routing.

- Deployment policy linked to budgets:
  - Canary windows remain allowed at Normal. At Elevated, only low-risk canaries for critical fixes. At High/Critical, no canaries except emergency-security/availability patches approved by SRE lead.

3) Capacity Planning
- Goals and targets:
  - Target steady-state utilization: 60% - 75% of provisioned serving capacity (GPU and CPU) to leave buffer for bursts and headroom for autoscaling.
  - Safety buffer: maintain a 15% headroom reserve in Dedicated pools for burst capacity; increase to 25% during major product launches.
  - Scaling objectives: scale-up decision should be triggered when 5-minute sustained utilization > 80% and predicted 1-hour load growth > 10%.

- Forecasting cadence and inputs:
  - Monthly forecast for next 3 months; quarterly for next 12 months. Inputs: traffic growth (real traffic & synthetic canary results), feature roadmaps (expected launches), historical CPU/GPU utilization, KV cache hit-rate, and model mix changes (larger models increase per-request GPU usage).
  - Owners: service/product manager provides demand forecast; SRE provides capacity plan and cost estimates.

- Autoscaling and provisioning rules:
  - Horizontal scaling preferred for stateless inference workers; vertical scaling (bigger GPUs) for throughput-heavy long-seq workloads only after perf benchmarking.
  - Autoscaler config standards (example): min_replicas=3, target_utilization=0.65, cooldown=120s, max_replicas=100.

4) Reliability Initiatives and Investment Process
- Initiative types:
  1. Systemic reliability fixes (root-cause fixes, kernel/IO improvements).
  2. Observability and playbook improvements (new metrics, dashboards, synthetic checks).
  3. Capacity and autoscaling improvements (better bin-packing, predictive scaling).
  4. Resilience features (graceful degradation, cached fallbacks, multi-region routing).

- Prioritization framework:
  - Score initiatives by user impact (customer-facing failure frequency * severity), cost to implement, and expected ROI (reduction in error budget burn / cost savings).
  - Quarterly OKR alignment: SRE allocates 30% of engineering cycles to reliability initiatives; remaining time for operational debt and platform improvements.

- Tracking and outcomes:
  - Each initiative has an owner, acceptance criteria, a measurable SLO impact target, and a go/no-go review at completion. Post-launch, measure change in error budget burn and tag relevant SLO metrics for 60 days.

5) Incident Review Standards
- Purpose: ensure consistent blameless postmortems that identify root causes, action items, and owners.

- Required timeline:
  - Major incidents (SLA impacting or > 25% monthly error budget): publish preliminary incident timeline within 48 hours; full postmortem within 7 calendar days.
  - Medium incidents: postmortem within 14 days.

- Postmortem template (must include):
  1. Incident summary (what happened, impact, customer-visible symptoms).
  2. Timeline of events (with UTC timestamps).
  3. Root cause analysis (technical and organizational).
  4. Immediate mitigations taken and why they worked/didn't.
  5. Action items (owner, ETA, verification criteria).
  6. Error budget impact (minutes burned) and follow-up verification plan.
  7. Lessons learned and preventative measures.

- Quality gate for postmortems:
  - SRE review board ensures postmortem includes a clear root cause, at least one actionable preventative measure, and assigned owner. Postmortems failing the quality gate must be updated within 3 business days.

6) Operational Tooling and Dashboards
- Required dashboards (per-service):
  - SLO dashboard: current SLO attainment, burn rate, historical 30-day window.
  - Capacity dashboard: GPU/CPU utilization, node health, queue lengths, autoscaler decisions.
  - Incident health: current pages, recent high-severity alerts, on-call rotation.

- Alerts and thresholds (examples):
  - Page when: error_rate > 0.5% sustained for 5m (for critical APIs), or p95 latency breach > 20% of SLO for 10m.
  - Warning when: error_rate > 0.2% sustained for 10m, or queue_length > 1000.

- Synthetic checks and canaries:
  - Maintain a multi-region synthetic suite testing primary customer flows (generation, chat + function calls, embeddings). Canary failures count as early-warning indicators and should be mapped to a low-severity alert that escalates if multiple regions fail.

- Tooling stack (standard):
  - Metrics: Prometheus (remote write to Grafana Cloud)
  - Dashboards/Alerts: Grafana + PagerDuty integration
  - Tracing: OpenTelemetry -> Jaeger or Tempo
  - Canary/Chaos: Grafana Cloud synthetics + Chaos Toolkit for controlled experiments

7) Runbook Standards and Examples
- Runbook format (required fields):
  - Title, scope, owner, pager role, pre-reqs (credentials), detection mechanism, immediate mitigation steps, escalation path, rollback instructions, verification steps, post-incident actions.

- Example: API 5xx surge runbook (condensed)
  1. Detection: PagerDuty alert "api-5xx-rate-high" triggered and SLO burn rate > 50%.
  2. Immediate mitigations (within 10m):
     - Confirm metrics: run PromQL queries for error rate and p95 latency.
       - promql: sum(rate(request_errors{job=\"api\"}[5m])) / sum(rate(request_total{job=\"api\"}[5m]))
     - Identify recent deploys in last 60m: curl -s https://deployments.redwood/api/recent?service=api
     - Rollback last non-security deploy: kubectl rollout undo deployment/api --to-revision=<last-stable> (owner must coordinate with release engineer).
     - If rollback not possible or does not help: scale up serving pool by +25%: kubectl scale deployment/api --replicas=$(($(kubectl get deployment api -o jsonpath='{.status.replicas}')*125/100))
  3. Escalation (if >30m unresolved): call Platform SRE and Product owner; open a conference bridge.
  4. Verification: run synthetic request suite and validate SLO metrics trending toward normal for at least 30m.
  5. Post-incident: create postmortem, schedule action-owner to complete permanent fix within agreed ETA.

- Runbook maintenance:
  - Runbooks reviewed quarterly by owners. Any runbook used in an incident must be updated within 5 business days to reflect lessons learned.

8) Ownership, Communication, and Governance
- Responsibility matrix:
  - Service owners: define service-specific SLOs (must conform to company standards or request exception), maintain runbooks, and own fixes.
  - SRE team: review proposed SLOs, operate incident response, maintain platform runbooks, and assist capacity planning.
  - Product managers: informed on significant budget burns and approve high-impact mitigation choices.

- Communication channels:
  - On-call paging via PagerDuty.
  - SLO and capacity reports: automated weekly digest to #sre-ops and monthly exec summary to leadership.

- Exceptions and review process:
  - Any deviation from these standards (SLOs lower than default or different error budget windows) requires a written exception request, service-level risk assessment, and approval from SRE lead and Product lead.

Appendices
A. Typical SLO Definitions (quick reference)
- Availability 99.95% -> 21.6 minutes/month
- Availability 99.9% -> 43.2 minutes/month
- Availability 99.99% -> 4.32 minutes/month

B. PromQL quick snippets
- p95 latency: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{job=\"api\"}[5m])) by (le))
- error rate: sum(rate(request_errors{job=\"api\"}[5m])) / sum(rate(request_total{job=\"api\"}[5m]))

C. Contacts (roles)
- Platform SRE lead: platform-sre@redwood.example.com
- On-call rotation: see /confluence/eng-sre/oncall-rotations
